title: Meeting Rooms — Overlap Counting and Minimum Resources
summary: Can one room host every meeting, and if not, how many rooms does peak concurrency actually require? Two related but distinct problems, both solved by tracking how many intervals are simultaneously active.

slides.markdown:
"Meeting Rooms" is actually two problems that share a name. **Meeting Rooms I** asks a yes/no question: can a single room host every meeting without conflict? **Meeting Rooms II** asks a harder one: what's the *minimum number of rooms* needed so nothing ever conflicts?

The first is a simple pairwise-overlap check after sorting. The second requires tracking **how many meetings are simultaneously active at any moment** — not just whether any two overlap, but the actual peak concurrency.

That concurrency-tracking idea is the real payload of this topic: it's the seed of the general **sweep line technique** the next topic builds out fully, and it reappears in Skyline and countless "how many X are active right now" problems outside intervals entirely.

slides.sectionTitle: Meeting Rooms I: one room, yes or no
Meeting Rooms II: how many meetings overlap at once
slides.markdown:
Knowing that *some* pair overlaps isn't enough to size a room count — you need the **maximum number of meetings active at the same instant**, anywhere across the whole schedule. That peak concurrency is exactly the minimum number of rooms required: if at some moment 3 meetings are simultaneously in progress, you need at least 3 rooms, and 3 is always sufficient too, since rooms free up as meetings end.

The technique: split every meeting into two separate events — a **start** (occupancy +1) and an **end** (occupancy −1) — sort all events by time, and sweep through tracking a running counter. The counter's maximum value across the whole sweep is the answer.

slides.sectionTitle: Two sorted arrays swept in lockstep
slides.markdown:
One clean implementation: pull out all start times into one sorted array and all end times into another, then walk both with two pointers, always advancing whichever is smaller. Each start pointer step means "a room is now occupied" (increment concurrency); each end pointer step means "a room just freed up" (decrement concurrency). Track the running maximum as you go.

slides.sectionTitle: The two-pointer sweep for minimum rooms
slides.markdown:
```python
def min_meeting_rooms(meetings):
    starts = sorted(m[0] for m in meetings)
    ends = sorted(m[1] for m in meetings)

    rooms = max_rooms = 0
    s = e = 0
    while s < len(starts):
        if starts[s] < ends[e]:
            rooms += 1          # a meeting starts, room count grows
            s += 1
        else:
            rooms -= 1          # a meeting ends first, room frees up
            e += 1
        max_rooms = max(max_rooms, rooms)

    return max_rooms
```

The two separately-sorted arrays cost O(n log n) to build; the sweep itself is O(n). Same overall complexity as Meeting Rooms I, but it answers a strictly harder question.

slides.sectionTitle: Two-array sweep vs a min-heap of end times
slides.markdown:
| | Two sorted arrays | Min-heap of end times |
|---|---|---|
| Idea | Sweep starts and ends in lockstep, track a counter | Sort by start; for each new meeting, pop any heap entries that have already ended, then push the new end time |
| Room count | The running max of the counter | The heap's size at any point (after popping stale entries) |
| Complexity | O(n log n) sort, O(n) sweep | O(n log n) — each meeting does one push and at most one pop |
| What it generalizes to | Sweep line (next topic) | Assigning specific room *identities*, not just a count |

Both answer "how many rooms," but the heap version naturally extends to "*which* meeting goes in *which* room" — pop the heap to find a free room, assign the meeting to it, push its new end time back. The two-array version only ever gives you the count.

slides.sectionTitle: A meeting ending at t is not the same as one starting at t
slides.markdown:
If meeting A ends at 10:00 and meeting B starts at 10:00, they should **not** count as simultaneously occupying a room — A has vacated by the time B begins. Using `starts[s] < ends[e]` (strict less-than) in the two-pointer sweep gets this right: when a start and an end tie exactly, the end is processed first, correctly freeing the room before counting the new occupancy.

Using `<=` instead would count both as active at once, inflating the room count by one whenever a meeting ends exactly when another begins — a subtle off-by-one that only shows up on back-to-back scheduling, which is common in real calendar data (people routinely book 9:00–10:00 followed immediately by 10:00–11:00).

slides.sectionTitle: This data is also a removal-count problem
slides.markdown:
The same overlap data underlies a differently-framed question: "Erase Overlap Intervals" asks for the **minimum number of intervals to remove** so none of the remaining ones overlap. That's not solved by tracking concurrency — it's solved by a **greedy, earliest-finish-time** strategy: always keep the interval that frees up the room soonest.

The exchange-argument proof for why earliest-finish-time greedy is optimal — and the general activity-selection framing behind it — is owned by [exchange-argument](exchange-argument) in the greedy group; it's worth reading once you've internalized the concurrency-counting side here, since the two techniques get reached for on visually similar-looking problems.

The running counter's maximum value isn't just an abstract number — it's a direct, physical answer: **the minimum number of interchangeable resources needed so nothing is ever forced to wait.**

This generalizes far past conference rooms: it's the same computation for the minimum number of parking spots a garage needs given arrival/departure times, the minimum number of concurrent database connections a pool must support given query durations, or the minimum number of worker threads needed to run a batch of overlapping jobs without queuing. Any time a resource is claimed for a duration and released, "peak concurrent claims" is this exact calculation.

slides.sectionTitle: The senior-level nuance: cost, not just count
slides.markdown:
A junior candidate stops at "the answer is the peak concurrency count." A senior candidate notes what the count *doesn't* capture: real rooms differ in **cost, capacity, and location**, so minimizing room count isn't always the actual business objective.

If rooms have different costs, this becomes an assignment problem — greedily reusing the cheapest available room (via the min-heap approach from earlier, picking the lowest-cost free room instead of any free room) rather than just counting how many are needed. If meetings have different sizes, you need capacity-aware bin-packing, which peak concurrency alone doesn't solve — you could have low concurrency but still need a large room for one huge meeting. Naming this distinction — "the count answers resource sizing, not resource selection" — is what separates a correct answer from a complete one.

Both variants are **O(n log n)** overall — the sort (whether one array or two, or building a heap) dominates a linear sweep. Space is O(n) for the sorted arrays or the heap.

Meeting Rooms I answers a yes/no question in a single adjacent-pair check. Meeting Rooms II answers a count, via a running concurrency counter over a full event sweep. Both are instances of the same idea: **turn interval endpoints into ordered events and scan them once** — which is precisely what the next topic generalizes into a named technique.
